content: 1. Tuberculosis (TB) preventive treatment may be provided following a clinical evaluation or in accordance with national guidelines. For selected high-risk household contacts of patients with multidrug-resistant TB, preventive treatment can be considered based on an individualized risk assessment and sound clinical justification. 2. Individuals initiating anti-TNF treatment, those undergoing dialysis, patients preparing for organ or hematological transplantation, and individuals with silicosis should be systematically tested and treated for latent TB infection (LTBI). 3. Systematic testing and treatment for LTBI may also be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from countries with a high TB burden, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. 4. Systematic LTBI testing and treatment are not recommended for individuals with diabetes, those who engage in harmful alcohol use, tobacco smokers, or underweight individuals unless they belong to other high-risk groups included in the above recommendations. 5. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those who do not report symptoms such as current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered preventive treatment, regardless of their antiretroviral therapy (ART) status. 6. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who report symptoms such as current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats during TB screening should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. If active TB is excluded, they should be offered preventive treatment. 7. Chest radiography may be offered to people living with HIV on ART. Preventive treatment should be provided to those without abnormal radiographic findings. 8. Infants and children living with HIV who exhibit poor weight gain, fever, current cough, or have a history of contact with a TB case should be evaluated for TB and other diseases causing such symptoms. If active TB is excluded after appropriate clinical evaluation or in accordance with national guidelines, these children should be offered TB preventive treatment, regardless of their age. 9. The absence of TB symptoms and abnormal chest radiographic findings can be used to rule out active TB disease among HIV-negative household contacts aged 5 years or older and other risk groups before initiating preventive treatment. 10. Either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) can be used to test for LTBI. However, LTBI testing is not a prerequisite for initiating preventive treatment in people living with HIV or child household contacts under 5 years of age. 11. The following treatment regimens are recommended for LTBI, regardless of HIV status: 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. Additionally, a 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or 4 months of daily rifampicin alone may be offered as alternatives. 12. For children and adolescents under 15 years of age in countries with high TB incidence, a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin or weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid for 3 months may be offered as alternatives to 6 months of isoniazid monotherapy. 13. In countries with low TB incidence, alternative regimens to 6 months of isoniazid monotherapy include 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, a 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid, 3–4 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin, or 3–4 months of rifampicin alone. 14. In settings with high TB transmission, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have an unknown or positive LTBI test and are unlikely to have active TB disease should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT). This should be provided regardless of ART status, degree of immunosuppression, history of previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. 15. Daily IPT for 36 months should be given in high TB transmission settings as defined by national authorities, irrespective of ART status, immunosuppression level, prior TB treatment history, or pregnancy.
